newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EP committee approves electricity liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EP committee approves electricity liberalisation.

text.p: The European Parliament's energy committee approved on Tuesday a report which paves the way for the partial liberalisation of the European Union electricity market.

"I am very pleased," Belgian Socialist rapporteur Claude Desama told Reuters after the committee vindicated his strategy on the draft electricity directive -- COM(93)643 -- and approved most of his amendments to the text.

Desama acknowledged EU energy ministers were likely to reject most of the amendments in December, when they are due to approve the draft directive, but he said that while the text could be improved it was acceptable as it stood.
He expected the full parliament to approve his report on the proposal on December 11.

The draft liberalisation directive has been the subject of heated debate between the EU member states for the last five years and the common position approved by EU energy ministers on June 20 strikes a delicate balance between the minimalist French and the maximalist British.

Anxious not to upset the balance and trigger a dispute between parliament and Council which could have prevented the directive getting onto the statute books at all, Desama persuaded the energy committee to demand only a limited number of amendments to the common position.

Most of these are of Desama's own making and reiterate requests made by MEPs when they gave the proposal its first reading in 1993, namely harmonisation of environmental and safety standards, and transparency of accounts which shows whether utilities are internalising their environmental costs and imposing acceptable prices on customers.
"These are the only important elements of the common position which are unsatisfactory," Desama said.

The rapporteur hopes to convince ministers to make concessions on these points in return for MEPs' support on the electricity directive and its sister directive on gas liberalisation, which the forthcoming Dutch presidency of the EU hopes to finalise before next summer.
He also wants the Council to agree to let local and regional authorities negotiate long-term supply contracts with the electricity distributors.

While ministers are unlikely to accept this, the demand is a pre-emptive strike designed eventually to eek more concessions out of the Council when it decides on the role of the distributors in the gas sector.
The EU is highly dependent on external gas supplies.

Desama, who has been named rapporteur on the gas directive, believes that the big EU gas buyers like Gaz de France and the Netherlands' Gasunie will only be able to protect their share of the distribution market from non-EU competitors if they are allowed to negotiate long-term take-or-pay contracts with the third country suppliers.

Ironically, these guarantees would have been better assured if the Council had accepted France's original proposal for a single buyer system as an alternative to negotiated third party access (TPA) to the electricity and gas networks, Desama said.
The French model, calqued on Electricite de France's existing role, dictated that all power contracts between suppliers and consumers would pass through a central buyer.

This offered the advantages of a monopoly without the disadvantages, at least for consumers, but the Council's attempts to ensure the system offered market openings equivalent to those provided by third party access to the grid have rendered it so complex that even EdF is likely to resort to TPA, Desama predicted happily.
"The (original) single buyer system would have been more justifiable in the gas sector, linked to obligatory long-term contracts," he said.

"But the Council can't go back to that now and France won't even want it because there is more than one French gas company. Elf Aquitaine wants a share of the market as well as Gaz de France," he pointed out.
